A magnitude 6.9 earthquake that struck Yushu, a Tibetan prefecture in Qinghai, China, on the morning of 14 April 2010. It killed about 2,700 people, most of them in the town of Gyêgu (Jyekundo), and left some 100,000 homeless on the Tibetan plateau, at about 3,700 metres.

Most houses in the town were built of mud brick and timber, and they collapsed, as did many schools. Monks from local monasteries were among the first to dig out survivors and to cremate the dead in mass funerals, scenes that drew attention across China and abroad. The thin air, the cold and the distance from big cities made rescue hard.

The government rebuilt the town within a few years as a planned city, with wide roads and new housing, which some residents felt erased its Tibetan character. Earthquakes are common here because India keeps pushing north into Asia; compare the Assam and Tibet earthquake of 1950 and the Sichuan earthquake of 2008. The Qinghai-Tibet Railway had linked the plateau to eastern China only four years before.
